name: Refugee Status Under the Law on Refugees

requirements.blocker_text: Written application must be submitted to a regional Department of Employment and Social Programs (under the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of Population) within 5 calendar days of arrival in Kazakhstan, or within 1 day for those who entered irregularly. After registering, the applicant receives an asylum-seeker certificate, attends an interview within 3 months, and receives a decision within 3 months (extendable up to 1 year for further review). Rejected applicants may appeal within 3 months through up to 3 court levels, with the Supreme Court as final instance.
requirements.fix_path: Register the asylum claim with the regional Department of Employment and Social Programs within the applicable deadline.

outcome.duration_length: indefinite, subject to periodic status review/extension

sources.title: UNHCR Central Asia -- describes Kazakhstan's domestic Law 'On Refugees': application deadlines (5 days/1 day for irregular entrants), the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of Population and regional Departments of Employment and Social Programs as the deciding authorities, interview/decision timelines, and a 3-level court appeal process for rejected claims

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Kazakhstan). STATUS: DRAFT -- sourced to UNHCR's own regional guidance (tier 2), not Kazakhstan's primary legal text (Kazakhstan's official government legal database, Adilet, almost certainly hosts the Law 'On Refugees' itself but the specific text was not located/fetched in this build; the closest attempted primary source, a UNECE conference paper, returned a 403 error). GENUINELY POSITIVE, DISTINCTIVE FINDING WORTH FOREGROUNDING GIVEN HOW RARE THIS IS IN THIS DATASET: Kazakhstan acceded to the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol in 1999 and operates an actual functioning domestic asylum law with defined timelines, a real government decision-making body, and -- notably -- a genuine judicial appeal path up to the Supreme Court for rejected applicants. This stands in sharp contrast to Lebanon (asylum law that's existed on paper since 1962 but used once), Tunisia (no domestic law, UNHCR mandate itself government-suspended), Kuwait (no domestic law or regulations at all), India/Pakistan/Sri Lanka (UNHCR mandate only, no domestic law) all built earlier in this dataset. Recognized refugees get 'freedom of employment in accordance with the legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan' and family reunification rights with spouse and dependent children -- work_rights and study_rights set 'full' on this basis, though the precise scope of any sector restrictions was not detailed in the source reviewed, so this should be treated as directionally strong rather than exhaustively verified.
